segments.say: Hugo is inside now, in his armchair by the window, a blanket over his knees. The family have come and gone in a cheerful rush of coats and goodnights, and the house is quiet again. He hasn't turned on the big light. Just the small lamp in the corner, and the soft sound of rain beginning again on the glass.

Let your attention come gently to your eyes. Whether they're open or closed, notice how they feel right now. Perhaps a little tired, a little warm, a little heavy. All evening, without asking, they've kept themselves moist and clear, blinking thousands of times to spread that thin, quiet film. Now they can rest. There's nothing more they need to look at.

If your eyes are still open, you might let your eyelids grow heavier, as if each blink is a little slower than the one before. There's no need to force them closed. Just let them drift down, as they would on a long, warm train journey, or in an armchair by a window. And if they're already closed, let them rest there, soft and still.

Let's soften the face, one small place at a time. The tiny muscles around the eyes, which squint and crease all day. The forehead, smoothing out like a sheet being shaken flat. The space between the eyebrows, where worry likes to gather. And the cheeks, loosening and settling, as if they've just stopped smiling after a long, happy evening.

show.title: Letting go, one place at a time
items: The small muscles around the eyes

segments.say: Now notice your jaw. Many of us hold it tight without realising, especially at the end of a long day. Let your teeth part just a little. Let your tongue rest softly in your mouth. Imagine the hinge of your jaw, just in front of your ears, loosening, as if someone has quietly oiled it. There's nothing to say now, and nothing to hold back.

Let your attention drift down to your throat. Earlier tonight, we talked about the lump in the throat that comes with being moved. Whatever feelings you've carried today, the throat doesn't need to hold them now. Let it be soft and open. Let each breath slide in and out easily, cool on the way in, warm on the way out.

A small lamp glowing beside a soft armchair, a folded blanket over one arm, raindrops on the dark window behind. Imagine yourself in a room like this, warm and safe, with nowhere you need to be. The rain is outside, and you're inside. That's all that matters for now.

show.cap: A lamp beside an armchair on a rainy night

segments.say: Now your shoulders. Let them drop, perhaps further than you expected. Imagine they've been carrying a heavy coat all day, wet from the rain, and now someone has gently lifted it away and hung it by the door. Feel the space that opens up between your shoulders and your ears. Breathe into that space, and let it widen a little more.

Let that heaviness flow down your arms, through your upper arms, past your elbows, into your forearms. Your arms might feel warm, or heavy, or simply still. Let your hands rest wherever they are, palms soft, fingers loose and slightly curled. There's nothing to hold, nothing to carry, nothing to fix. Your hands have done enough for today.

Let's take a few slow breaths together. Breathe in, just a little fuller than usual. A gentle pause at the top, without straining. And out, a little longer than the in-breath, as if you're sighing very quietly. Again. In, a little fuller. Pause. And out, slowly. Let the breath find its own pace again now. You don't need to count.

Notice the gentle rise and fall of your chest. Perhaps there's a little warmth there, the same warmth that comes with being moved by something kind. Let it spread, slowly, like the light of a single lamp in a dark room. Your heart is beating steadily, as it always does, without any help from you. You can simply let it.

Let your belly soften too. With each breath in, it rises a little, and with each breath out, it falls. There's a slow tide in it, like water in a canal lock, rising and settling, rising and settling. No need to make it deeper or slower. Just notice it moving on its own, the way water moves under a quiet bridge at night.

If thoughts come, and they will, that's perfectly all right. Let them drift past like ducks on the dark water of a canal. You can notice them, and let them float on downstream. You don't need to follow them or chase them away. Sooner or later each one will slip out of sight beneath a bridge, and the water will be still again.

There's nothing left to do tonight. No messages to answer. No problems to solve. No one to impress. Whatever you did today, it's finished now. Whatever didn't get done can wait until tomorrow, when you'll be rested. For now, the only thing being asked of you is to rest, and even that will happen by itself, in its own time.

Let the heaviness move down through your hips and into your legs. Your thighs grow heavy, sinking into whatever is beneath you. Your knees soften. Your calves loosen. And finally your feet, warm and still, as if they've just taken off a pair of wet boots after a long walk home. Let your whole body be held now, completely, by the bed or chair beneath you.

Now feel your whole body at once, from the top of your head to the tips of your toes. Heavy and warm. Soft and still. Held. There's nothing you need to do to stay here. The rain keeps falling softly outside. The lamp glows in the corner. And somewhere far away, a canal flows slowly through the dark, under one bridge after another.

There's only this now. Breath, coming and going. Warmth, gathered under the blanket. Stillness, spreading slowly from the inside out. Nothing to add and nothing to take away. If you notice the sound of the words, let them be soft and far away, like voices drifting from another room as you begin to fall asleep.
